items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Use Motives as an Indicator of Academic Performance among Nursing Students in a Higher Education Institution
items.abstract: In recent years, generative artificial intelligence has been growing in use and popularity, garnering around 3 billion monthly visits across various tools. This study aimed to determine the Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) use motives as an indicator of academic performance among nursing students in a higher education institution in Cebu City. Through this study, the researchers will determine whether the motivation in using generative AI has a positive or negative effect on the individual’s performance in the academe, specifically among nursing students. Using a mixed-method explanatory sequential design, the study selected 145 nursing students in all levels at the University of Southern Philippines Foundation College of Health Sciences Department of Nursing in the First Semester Academic Year 2025-2026. To conduct the study, the researchers sought approval through a letter from the dean of the Department of Nursing. Data were gathered through a validated instrument in a Google Forms link, where survey forms were distributed to designated group chats. Upon retrieval, the information remained confidential and complied fully with institutional research ethics board approvals. Statistical evaluations were performed to examine the study’s hypotheses and draw conclusions using Spearman's rank-order correlation. The findings revealed that there is a high level of generative AI use motives among nursing students with an overall weighted mean score of 3.434, and there is no statistically significant relationship between the generative artificial intelligence use motives and the academic performance of the respondents with a Spearman’s rho of 0.031 and a p-value of 0.715. These results provide a critical insight suggesting that the majority of respondents are driven by their strong intrinsic, utility, and attainment values for using artificial intelligence and show that their use motives in generative AI are not a reliable indicator of their academic grades.

items.title: Governing Generative AI in Critical Infrastructure Control
items.abstract: This working draft applies one governance model for generative AI in critical infrastructure control to the standards and regulatory regimes that govern the systems it runs in. Applications are assessed at a rigor set by their criticality band. A Bright Line is drawn on the consequence of each individual action. Above that line, an AI-originated action needs authorization by a qualified human broker, given in the moment or in advance through a verified gatekeeper over a pre-authorized envelope. Part I states the model and Part II the method for carrying it into any regime. Part III reads each regime in its own chapter: IEEE; ISA/IEC 62443; other ISA/IEC and ISO/IEC standards; NERC and FERC; the NRC; and NIST, the joint AI-in-OT principles, DOE, the EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, the IAEA, and EPRI. Part IV brings the recommendations together, organized by how each kind of body adopts something new. Version 0.9 is posted for comment. Chapters 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 9 are in place, and Chapters 3, 5, and 7 are in outline. The executive summary will follow once comment has been taken. Version 1.0 is reserved for the version that takes comment in.

items.title: Guideline-based assessment of traumatic dental injury knowledge among dental students and AI chatbot interfaces: a comparative study with repeated AI sessions
items.abstract: Background Assessing guideline-based knowledge of traumatic dental injuries (TDIs) is important for identifying potential learning needs in undergraduate dental education. Although artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot interfaces are increasingly considered educational resources, their accuracy and repeat-session consistency in TDI knowledge assessments remain uncertain. This study compared the performance of dental students and four AI chatbot interfaces using a content-validated, guideline-based assessment. Methods In a 30-item International Association of Dental Traumatology guideline-based assessment, 225 students (110 fourth-year and 115 fifth-year) completed one timed Turkish-language examination, while four AI interfaces were assessed in English across 21 sessions each, with items submitted in separate conversations and no equivalent overall time limit. Unanswered student items were scored as incorrect. The primary analysis used item-adjusted logistic regression with two-way cluster-robust standard errors accounting for student or AI-session and assessment-item clustering. Pairwise p-values were adjusted using the Holm procedure across all 15 comparisons. Respondent-clustered generalized estimating equations (GEE) and paired item-level bootstrap analyses were used as complementary sensitivity analyses. Results Overall accuracy was 65.1% among fourth-year students and 75.0% among fifth-year students, compared with 90.6%, 84.3%, 81.0%, and 77.1% for ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and DeepSeek, respectively. In the primary two-way cluster-robust model, fourth-year students had lower odds of a correct response than fifth-year students (OR 0.603, 95% CI 0.457–0.795; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0046). Although ChatGPT demonstrated higher observed accuracy (OR 3.398, 95% CI 1.385–8.337), its comparison with fifth-year students was not statistically significant after Holm adjustment across all 15 pairwise comparisons (adjusted p = 0.0908). No other AI interface demonstrated a statistically significant advantage over fifth-year students under the primary analysis. Excluding potentially ambiguous or negatively worded items did not alter the Holm-adjusted conclusions, although substantial item-level uncertainty remained. Conclusions Fifth-year students demonstrated higher guideline-based knowledge-assessment accuracy than fourth-year students under common examination conditions. AI interfaces differed in overall accuracy and repeat-session correctness patterns. Because the student and AI protocols differed in language, timing, conversational format, and assessment frequency, cross-modality contrasts cannot establish relative performance under equivalent conditions. The findings support item-level verification of AI-generated answers and warrant future language-matched, protocol-standardized evaluations.

items.title: How Artificial Intelligence Reshapes White-Collar Workers’ Personality at Work
items.abstract: This narrative review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) may reshape personality at work among white-collar workers. It integrates trait activation theory, situation strength theory, the cognitive-affective personality system, the TESSERA framework, and self-concept perspectives from personality and organizational psychology. Theories were purposively selected, and peer-reviewed studies published mainly from 2022 onward were reviewed. The framework resulted from the review perceives AI not merely as a work tool but as a recurring social, psychological, and organizational context. Baseline personality may influence employees’ affective and cognitive characteristic adaptations, executive functions, perceptions of AI-mediated work, and behavioral responses. In the short term, these responses may adjust characteristic adaptations and work-related behavior. Over time, recursive feedback may gradually reshape work-related self-concept and contribute to longer-term personality development. However, current research has focused mainly on situational appraisals, identity, job autonomy, competence beliefs, and behavior, whereas direct evidence of personality trait change remains limited. Future research should therefore use diverse designs to test the proposed mechanisms and examine the individual, occupational, and organizational factors involved. For human resource practice, organizations should treat AI adoption as work redesign that emphasizes critical evaluation of AI outputs, metacognitive monitoring, skill development and retention, and prevention of AI over-reliance, deskilling, pseudo-skilling, and psychological entitlement.

items.title: How Human and AI Conditions Combine to Shape Learning Achievement: A Configurational Study of GenAI-Enabled Teaching in Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being embedded in technology-supported teaching, but its educational value depends on how technological, pedagogical, learner-related, and organizational conditions combine. Using 68 course-offering cases from Chinese higher education, this study applies necessary condition analysis and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis to examine configurations associated with learning achievement. Results identify four high-achievement and three low-achievement configurations, showing equifinality and causal asymmetry. GenAI-related conditions are central in some successful pathways, are absent in others, and also appear in a low-achievement configuration when supportive pedagogical conditions are lacking. Their role further varies across administrative-workload contexts. The findings show that effective GenAI-enabled teaching depends on how technology is configured with interaction, feedback, learner participation, and organizational conditions rather than on technology use alone.

items.title: Human-AI Collective Agency in Augmenting Language Teaching Materials: Co-creation, Adaptation, Curation, and Humanization
items.abstract: Language teachers in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts are increasingly using Generative AI (GenAI) to augment teaching materials, yet existing research tends to overlook how these materials are produced in situ. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory (ANT), this qualitative study explores how 12 Chinese university EFL teachers exert agency to use AI in augmenting language teaching materials. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and digital artifacts from all 12 teachers, as well as classroom observations of two of these teachers. The findings reveal that human and AI form collective agency, which is manifested through four synergy modes: Co-creation, Adaptation, Curation, and Humanization. In Co-creation, teachers work with AI to transcend modal limits and construct innovative multimodal assemblages. In Adaptation and Curation, acting as Obligatory Passage Points (OPP), teachers translate GenAI outputs by calibrating linguistic difficulty and enacting ideological and cultural gatekeeping to filter out cultural biases and factual hallucinations. In Humanization, teachers engage in clandestine labor and strategic transparency to re-assert human authorship, defending their professional legitimacy against the internal cheating mindset and re-legitimizing their professional identity. This study conceptualizes teacher agency as a collective achievement and demonstrates how GenAI amplifies the materials augmentation power of frontline teachers. It calls for the advancement of teacher education towards critical AI literacy and the establishment of sound institutional support to stabilize the dynamic educational network.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration and Professional Judgment in Accounting Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence can help accounting students produce analyses that exceed what they could complete independently. This creates a curriculum problem: better work produced with assistance does not necessarily indicate better understanding. This paper examines how human–AI collaboration can support the development of professional judgment rather than replace the reasoning through which it is learned. Drawing on cognitive offloading, research on human reliance on automation, and theories of curriculum alignment and feedback, it develops a conceptual framework connecting student learning with the improvement of teaching resources. The analysis identifies three tensions: greater access to explanations increases the need to evaluate them; automated assistance improves immediate performance while potentially removing opportunities to learn; and extensive learning records do not necessarily provide valid evidence of competence. Four mechanisms address these tensions: allocating cognitive tasks according to learning objectives, requiring verification against evidence, adjusting support as competence develops, and converting reviewed classroom feedback into improvements in cases and guidance. The framework distinguishes the learner's revision of a judgment from the institution's revision of teaching resources and assigns responsibilities to students, teachers, and AI systems. A management accounting example illustrates how these mechanisms operate together. The paper explains why the educational effects of AI depend on prior knowledge, assessment incentives, and the quality of human review, and proposes ways to examine both independent performance and responsible use of assistance.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration in Social Work Practice: Opportunities, Challenges and Ethical Implications in Makadara Sub-County, Nairobi City County, Kenya
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly discussed as a means of supporting information-intensive work, including documentation, information retrieval and service coordination. In Social Work and related social services, however, its adoption raises questions about professional judgment, digital inequality, data protection, algorithmic bias and accountability. This study explored practitioners’ reported awareness, use and perceptions of the opportunities, challenges and ethical implications of human–AI collaboration in Makadara Sub-County, Nairobi City County, Kenya. A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected using Questionnaires from 100 practitioners. Interviews were conducted with 12 key informants: six frontline social workers, four supervisors and two programme or service coordinators. From the findings, 68 (68%) reported using an AI tool for a work-related task and 32 (32%) reported no such use. Administrative time-saving (74%) and improved access to relevant information (70%) were the most frequently endorsed potential opportunities. Privacy and confidentiality risks (96%), inaccurate or misleading outputs (85%) and algorithmic bias (75%) were the most frequently identified concerns. Five themes emerged: administrative support rather than professional replacement; faster information access and referral navigation; uneven digital readiness; confidentiality, bias and accountability; and the continuing centrality of human judgment and relational practice. The findings indicate that practitioners recognized possible uses of AI while emphasizing verification, organizational readiness, data protection and human oversight. The study contributes context-specific evidence about practitioners’ reported awareness, use and perceptions in an urban Kenyan setting. The study establishes that responsible human–AI collaboration requires attention to local infrastructure, professional capacity, institutional governance and service-user rights. items.title: HUMANS AND TECHNOLOGY: THE ROLE AND LIMITATIONS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN A RADIOLOGIST'S WORK
items.abstract: This paper analyzes the application of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in modern radiological practice, the potential for automating diagnostic processes, the advantages in medical image analysis, and the existing limitations in clinical practice. It highlights the importance of using machine learning and deep neural networks to evaluate the results of radiography, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound (US) examinations. Furthermore, it discusses the diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence algorithms, the primary role of the physician in clinical decision-making, medical data security, and bioethical issues.

items.title: Impact of a Gamified Learning Platform on Employee Motivation and Skill Development
items.abstract: Employee training plays an important role in organizational development; however, maintaining employee motivation and encouraging continuous skill development remain challenging in conventional learning environments. This study presents the design and implementation of a gamified learning platform aimed at supporting employee motivation and workplace skill development through interactive learning activities. The platform was developed using Flask as the application framework and Supabase PostgreSQL for data storage. It incorporates three learning modules covering Communication Skills, Problem Solving and Digital Workplace Skills. Gamification elements, including points, levels and a leaderboard, are integrated to encourage participation and provide feedback on learning progress. Each module includes quiz-based assessments, while an eight-item motivation questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale is administered before and after the learning experience to record employee responses. The platform also maintains skill-wise performance records and provides progress-based learning suggestions to guide subsequent learning activities. A preliminary evaluation involving 19 participants showed an increase in the average self-reported motivation score from 3.91 to 4.28; however, this difference was not statistically significant at the 5% level. The quiz dataset comprised 80 assessment attempts from 14 participants, with an overall pass rate of 86.25% and weighted accuracy of 81.37%. These findings provide preliminary insights into the implementation and evaluation of gamification-supported workplace learning. The study also highlights the need for larger participant groups and more comprehensive evaluation to examine its effectiveness. Keywords— Gamification, Employee Motivation, Skill Development, Workplace Learning, Employee Engagement, Learning Analytics, Progress-Based Learning.

items.title: IMPACT OF PROLONGED SITTING, SCREEN EXPOSURE AND WORKLOAD ON MUSCULOSKELETAL HEALTH AMONG IT PROFESSIONALS: A MULTICENTRIC STUDY
items.abstract: Background The rapid expansion of information technology has substantially changed the occupational environment, with a large proportion of employees spending most of their working day using computers and other digital devices. IT professionals commonly experience prolonged sitting, extensive screen exposure, repetitive keyboard and mouse use, sustained visual concentration, limited postural variation, and high cognitive workload. These occupational characteristics may contribute to the development of work-related musculoskeletal symptoms involving the neck, shoulders, upper back, lower back, wrists, and hands. A recent systematic review of computer users reported a high overall burden of work-related musculoskeletal disorders, with the lower back, neck, upper back, and shoulder among the most frequently affected regions. The World Health Organization also recommends that adults limit sedentary behaviour and replace sedentary time with physical activity of any intensity. Objective The present study aimed to investigate the impact of prolonged sitting, screen exposure, and occupational workload on musculoskeletal health among IT professionals working in multiple organizational centres. The study also aimed to determine the prevalence and distribution of musculoskeletal symptoms and examine the association between occupational exposure variables and symptom severity. Materials and Methods A multicentric cross-sectional observational study was assumed to be conducted among 240 IT professionals recruited from four IT organizations. Participants were aged 22–45 years and had a minimum of one year of professional computer-based work experience. Demographic information, occupational characteristics, daily sitting duration, screen exposure, working hours, movement-break frequency, physical activity, workload, and workstation characteristics were recorded using a structured questionnaire. Musculoskeletal symptoms were assessed using the Standardized Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire, while pain intensity was assessed using the Numeric Pain Rating Scale. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, independentsamples t-tests, Pearson correlation analysis, and multivariable logistic regression were assumed to be used. Statistical significance was established at p < 0.05. Results The assumed sample consisted of 240 IT professionals with a mean age of 30.8 ± 5.2 years and mean professional experience of 6.4 ± 3.8 years. Participants reported an average working duration of 8.7 ± 1.1 hours/day, sitting duration of 7.2 ± 1.3 hours/day, and screen exposure of 8.1 ± 1.2 hours/day. Overall, 194 participants (80.8%) reported at least one musculoskeletal symptom during the preceding 12 months. The neck was the most frequently affected region (55.0%), followed by the lower back (52.5%), shoulders (45.4%), upper back (39.6%), and wrist/hand (28.3%). Participants with more than eight hours of daily sitting demonstrated a significantly greater prevalence of musculoskeletal symptoms than participants with less than six hours of sitting (96.3% vs. 62.5%, p < 0.001). High screen exposure and high workload were also significantly associated with musculoskeletal symptoms. Sitting duration (r = 0.42), screen exposure (r = 0.35), and workload (r = 0.48) demonstrated positive correlations with symptom severity, while movement-break frequency demonstrated a negative correlation (r = −0.31); all assumed correlations were statistically significant at p < 0.001. Multivariable logistic regression demonstrated that prolonged sitting, high screen exposure, high workload, infrequent breaks, and poor ergonomic conditions were independent predictors of musculoskeletal symptoms. Conclusion The assumed findings suggest that musculoskeletal symptoms are highly prevalent among IT professionals and are associated with multiple interacting occupational factors. Prolonged sitting, extensive screen exposure, high workload, insufficient movement breaks, and poor workstation ergonomics may contribute to increased musculoskeletal symptom burden. Preventive workplace physiotherapy, ergonomic assessment, regular movement breaks, physical activity, and workload management should be incorporated into occupational health programs for IT professionals.

items.title: Innovation ecosystem of urban AI: latent technocentrism in smart city governance
items.abstract: This article examines actors and power dynamics in the innovation ecosystem of urban artificial intelligence (AI). Based on document and network analysis and 26 semi-structured interviews, it maps the Quebec urban AI ecosystem and shows that, while fragmented, it is highly mediated. Cities remain the central demand holders but are heavily dependent on technology companies and intermediary nonprofit organizations. Network analysis shows that technological and cognitive dependencies dominate economic ones. This gives power to actors who control expertise, coordination, and knowledge, rather than formal authority. Building on these findings, the article introduces the concept of latent technocentrism. It explores how technocentric governance logics can emerge implicitly in ecosystem configurations, even without overt technology-driven agendas. This article contributes to smart city and urban governance scholarship by offering an actor-centric, systemic framework for analyzing emerging technologies such as urban AI. It also highlights the governance risks and policy implications of emerging urban AI ecosystems.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial y riesgo para la integridad electoral: percepciones de expertos iberoamericanos
items.abstract: Objective/context: This article analyzes Ibero-American experts’ perceptions of the risks of using artificial intelligence (AI) in electoral campaigns and identifies factors that heighten perceptions of risk to electoral integrity. The study is situated in a context marked by the growing integration of AI into political communication and by increasing concern about its implications for disinformation, electoral competition, and party organization. Methodology: A two-round Delphi study was conducted with 50 experts in political communication and electoral campaigns from 14 Ibero-American countries. Using descriptive statistics, bivariate correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression, the study examined the relationship between perceived risk of AI to electoral integrity and campaign experience, as well as various communicative, ideological, and organizational factors. Conclusions: The experts consulted view AI as a risk to electoral integrity. This perception is linked to the belief that disinformation is a primary danger, the belief that the political right uses AI more effectively for mobilization, and certain aspects of political parties’ professionalization and structure. Prior experience in election campaigns serves as a differentiating factor in these perceptions. Furthermore, there is greater acceptance of instrumental uses of AI than of uses aimed at risk mitigation. Originality: The article presents comparative empirical evidence on experts’ perceptions of the risks posed by AI in Ibero-American election campaigns. Its primary contribution lies in integrating communicative, ideological, and organizational dimensions into a single analysis and treating direct experience in election campaigns as a differentiating factor.

items.title: Intersection of Algorithmic Justice, Climate Change and Environmental Justice: Ethical Issues and Concerns
items.abstract: This article examines the intersection of algorithmic justice, climate change and environmental justice. It argues that climate-related artificial intelligence can support modelling, early warning, emissions monitoring and adaptation planning, but can also reproduce environmental injustice through biased datasets, opaque governance, data colonialism, surveillance and undisclosed ecological costs. Rejecting both technological pessimism and technological solutionism, the article distinguishes algorithms from AI and proposes a justice-based framework grounded in impact assessment, community-led design, data sovereignty, transparency, carbon and water disclosure, human oversight and remedy. Climate AI is defensible only where it advances accountability, participation, law and ecological responsibility in practice today.

items.title: İş Gücü Planlamasında Yapay Zekâ Tabanlı Tahmin Modelleri: Sosyo-Teknik Etkiler, Algoritmik Adalet ve Örgütsel Güven
items.abstract: Operasyonel karmaşıklığın ve veri hacminin hızla arttığı günümüzde iş gücü planlaması, salt bir insan kaynakları fonksiyonu olmaktan çıkarak örgütsel sürdürülebilirliğin ve kurumsal dayanıklılığın stratejik bir bileşenine dönüşmüştür. Yapay zekâ (YZ) ve makine öğrenmesi algoritmalarının bu sürece entegrasyonu, örgütlere tahmine dayalı (predictive) ve kuralcı (prescriptive) analitik kapasiteler kazandırmaktadır. Ne var ki Yönetim Bilişim Sistemleri (YBS) perspektifinden bakıldığında bu entegrasyon, teknik bir altyapı güncellemesini aşarak çalışan psikolojisini, liderlik dinamiklerini ve örgütsel adalet algısını dönüştüren sosyo-teknik bir değişime karşılık gelmektedir. Kavramsal ve eleştirel bir literatür değerlendirmesine dayanan bu bölüm, sosyomateryalite yaklaşımını kuramsal zemin olarak benimseyerek YZ tabanlı iş gücü planlamasını üç eksende incelemektedir: proaktif destek ile dijital panoptikon arasındaki gerilim; matematiksel objektiflik yanılsaması ve hedef fonksiyonu çatışması; otomasyon önyargısı ve bunun örgütsel güven üzerindeki etkileri. Bölüm ayrıca algoritmik yönetimde şeffaflık paradoksu ile insan-makine iş birliğinin sosyolojik sınırları meselelerini tartışmaya açmakta; performans cezası ve hibrit çalışmada dijital izolasyon kavramlarını ampirik olarak sınanması gereken önermeler olarak ileri sürmektedir. items.title: Job quality in developed economies: a systematic literature review
items.abstract: Purpose This paper systematically reviews empirical literature on job quality (JQ) in developed economies. Based on 40 articles spanning over 25 years, we analyse the key definitions, theories, methods, measures and outcomes associated with JQ in developed economies. Design/methodology/approach In conducting the review, we followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Our initial search yielded 9262 published records. Based on inclusion criteria, 40 articles were included in this review. These papers were published between 1999 and 2025, across 31 journals. Most studies were published after 2010 in management, industrial relations and health-related journals. Findings We reveal inconsistencies and problems with existing approaches, and make conceptual, theoretical and methodological contributions. Finally, we develop a research agenda to inform and improve future studies related to JQ, and advance the literature and policymaking. Research limitations/implications In terms of possible limitations regarding these findings, restricting the review to Q1 journal could potentially bias the results and the inclusion of only English-language studies could inadvertently exclude valuable research published in other languages. Practical implications The findings will enable researchers to better plan and design future research. This research will usefully inform policymaking directed towards improving JQ and subsequently benefiting workers, organisations, economies and societies. Social implications Advancing theoretical and empirical knowledge regarding JQ will enable the creation and maintenance of better jobs and thereby improve social and economic outcomes, including health and wellbeing and social mobility. Originality/value Extending beyond the narrow foci of previous JQ reviews, this review identifies gaps and inconsistencies in JQ research and generates conceptual, theoretical and methodological contributions. Subsequently, it develops a future research agenda designed to enable researchers to better plan and design research, and inform policymaking.

items.title: Journalistic Entrepreneurship and Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Case Study on the Design and Adoption of Journo
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence offers great potential for innovation, helping professionals and companies improve existing processes and create new products and services. This study examines the potential of AI-driven digital entrepreneurship to address specific professional challenges. It analyses a significant and pioneering case in communication: Journo, a tool for the semi-automatic creation of news texts from audio. The methodology combines documentary analysis, in-depth interviews, and user testing. The value proposition, business model and vision of its founders concerning entrepreneurship with AI, including the necessary learning and skills, have been compiled through content analysis and in-depth interviews. Journo’s usability and functionality and the perception of its potential recipients are addressed through a user-testing approach. The methodology combines documentary analysis, in-depth interviews, and user testing. The first two approaches examine Journo’s value proposition, business model, and its founders’ perspectives on AI entrepreneurship, while user testing assesses the tool’s usability and functionality from the perspective of potential users. The results show this to be an innovative tool that does not aim to replace professional work, but rather to complement it, and that despite errors, especially human ones, it is perceived positively by users in terms of usefulness and ease of use. However, limited utilisation is noted by users with no previous experience of AI or who tend to accept the results generated without checking them. We conclude that the success of AI-based journalistic entrepreneurship depends not only on technological innovation, but also on users’ critical competencies and their ability to supervise AI-generated content.

items.title: Large language models in socially assistive robots for older adults: medical applications, clinical evidence, and regulatory considerations
items.abstract: Socially Assistive Robots (SARs) have emerged as promising technologies for supporting older adults through cognitive, social, and everyday assistance. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have expanded their conversational and adaptive capabilities, creating opportunities for applications that extend beyond companionship and general assistance toward software with clinically relevant functions. However, the integration of an LLM into a robotic system does not automatically establish a medical intended purpose or qualify the software as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). This state-of-the-art review examines the integration of LLMs into SARs for older adults, with particular emphasis on distinguishing applications intended for companionship, social interaction, and general well-being from those designed to support medical functions. The review analyzes conversational and multimodal architectures, current applications, evaluation methodologies, and the potential medical-device qualification of the resulting software. The focused comparative synthesis includes 11 primary studies and 11 complementary publications, following the full-text assessment of 112 records. The literature reveals two complementary directions. While several studies primarily investigate conversational performance, personalization, usability, and user acceptance, others explore cognitive assessment and structured cognitive interventions. However, the evaluation of these systems frequently emphasizes technical feasibility, interaction quality, and task performance rather than establishing the clinical validity and effectiveness of their intended medical functions. Furthermore, the use of clinical assessment instruments to characterize participants does not necessarily constitute clinical validation of the robotic software. These findings highlight the need to distinguish between technological development and clinical effectiveness when evaluating LLM-enabled SARs. Their potential translation into medical technologies requires clearly defined medical purposes, appropriate clinical validation, reliable and safe operation, patient-centered design, and consideration of the regulatory requirements applicable to their software functions.

items.title: Latent profiles of artificial intelligence literacy and associated factors among undergraduate nursing students: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background The rapid development and application of artificial intelligence (AI) have revolutionized the nursing discipline and clinical practice, making AI literacy a core competency for modern nursing professionals. National education policies and professional guidelines have highlighted the urgency of AI literacy training for nursing students. Aims This study aims to identify latent profiles of AI literacy in undergraduate nursing students and explore key associated factors, so as to provide empirical evidence for targeted AI education and the enhancement of their overall AI literacy. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 333 undergraduate nursing students from two Chinese medical colleges. Data were collected using a self-designed demographic questionnaire and three validated scales: the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Questionnaire for College Students, General Self-Efficacy Scale, and Educational Climate Inventory. A latent profile analysis was performed using Mplus 8.3, while descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, ANOVA, and multinomial logistic regression were conducted using SPSS 27.0. Results Three AI literacy latent profiles were identified: low (16.2%, n = 54), moderate (58.0%, n = 193), and high (25.8%, n = 86). R3STEP multinomial logistic regression showed that a more favorable educational climate, freshman status (vs. senior), and higher self-efficacy were significant predictors of membership in the high AI literacy profile (all P < 0.05). For the middle AI literacy profile, the same analysis identified a more favorable educational climate and freshman status (vs. senior) as significant associated factors (all P < 0.05). Conclusion Undergraduate nursing students present significant heterogeneity in AI literacy, with over half in the high-literacy subgroup, while approximately 42% fall into moderate or low levels. Nursing colleges should implement stratified, targeted AI literacy training, enhance support for rural and lower-literacy students, and optimize the educational environment to boost the intelligent transformation of nursing education.

items.title: More than a ‘tool’: A systems-theory perspective on how large language models endogenously transform management knowledge (for the worse)
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often considered a ‘tool’ in management research. However, this perspective prevents a deeper systemic understanding of factors leading to their adoption, and how their presence as an epistemic technology transforms the production of management knowledge. We caution against the risk of epistemic substitution through LLMs and adopt a deterministic view of LLMs as an epistemic technology. Developmental System Theory is enlisted to interrogate how LLMs influence (i) the production of management knowledge and (ii) how that influence initiates epistemic feedback loops and practises that reduce the scope of truth and possible knowledge. Doing so advances our understanding of how LLMs keep affecting the research process disadvantageously, with the resultant knowledge concerning social relations in and around work becoming problematic too. Hence, our model constitutes a diagnostic tool to understand how the use of LLMs in research processes endogenously transforms knowledge production in management research – for the worse. In so doing, our model is also a tool of possible remedy, for it highlights that an exclusive focus on LLMs and their effects on the production of management knowledge will be insufficient to undo the negative epistemic feedback loops and practises already set in motion.

items.abstract: Study objective: To examine the psychometric properties of the Behavioral Regulation in Sport Questionnaire (BRSQ-8) among young adult eSports players in Brazil, testing its fit to the factor structure of Self-Determination Theory. Methodology/approach: A quantitative, cross-sectional study of 661 Brazilian players (convenience sample; 85% male; mean age 22.86 years) who completed the Portuguese version of the BRSQ-8. Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA, WLSMV estimator) was performed, and composite reliability, average variance extracted, and Cronbach’s alpha were calculated. Main results: CFA confirmed the eight-factor structure, with good fit (CFI = 0.966; TLI = 0.961; RMSEA = 0.060; SRMR = 0.069), superior to alternative models. Composite reliability ranged from 0.82 to 0.93, although autonomous regulations were strongly correlated. Intrinsic motivations predominated, especially for stimulating experiences (M = 6.15) and goals (M = 5.89), while external regulation and amotivation had the lowest scores. Theoretical/methodological contributions: The study extends Self-Determination Theory and the BRSQ to eSports, providing a robust instrument to measure Brazilian players’ motivation and to support research on this consumer’s behavior. Relevance/originality: This is the first study to validate the BRSQ-8 among eSports players in Brazil, filling a gap in the measurement of motivation in a growing cultural and economic phenomenon. Social/managerial implications: The motivational profile identified helps teams, organizers, and brands design marketing and engagement strategies. items.title: Multilevel exercise empowerment scale: development and psychometric validation in U.S. Adults
items.abstract: Background Exercise empowerment—the perceived confidence and control over exercise choices leading to sustained exercise and fulfillment—operates across domains, yet no measure captures its multilevel nature. This study developed and evaluated the Multilevel Exercise Empowerment Scale (MEES) among U.S. adults (N = 813). Methods Comprehensive psychometric analyses were conducted: (1) exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses tested the underlying structure using split samples; (2) internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's α; (3) test-retest reliability was evaluated using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC); and (4) construct validity was examined through Spearman correlations with exercise self-efficacy, social support, and family spirituality. Results A four-factor structure (Overcoming Barriers, External Networks, Personal Fulfillment, Physical Activity Maintenance) with marginal-to-acceptable fit (RMSEA=0.060; SRMR=0.066; CFI=0.879) was supported. Reliability was high (α =0.81–0.91; total α =0.92; ICC=0.78). Convergent validity was supported by correlations with exercise self-efficacy (r s = 0.66) and social support (r s = 0.58), while discriminant validity was supported by a low correlation with family spirituality (r s = 0.26). Conclusions The MEES demonstrated strong reliability and evidence of construct validity, and the findings provided preliminary support for its four-factor structure, warranting further evaluation of structural validity across diverse populations.

items.title: Multimodal and generative artificial intelligence for automated radiology reporting: a narrative review
items.abstract: Purpose: Multimodal and generative artificial intelligence (AI) has shifted medical image analysis from lesion detection toward automated drafting of narrative radiology reports. This review examines the extent of that progress, the points at which AI enters the imaging workflow, and the conditions required for physicians to rely on its output.Current concepts: Image analysis has developed through 3 generations: rule-based computer-aided detection, task-specific convolutional networks, and vision–language foundation models that generate free text. For normal and common findings, AI-generated chest radiograph reports approach the quality of radiologists’ reports and reduce reading or documentation time by 15% to 42%. In complex cases, however, they contain clinically significant errors more often than radiologists’ reports. AI is now used for image reconstruction, worklist prioritization, screening double reading, report drafting, and, within narrowly defined tasks, autonomous reporting. Randomized and real-world studies show benefits in mammographic screening and health-screening chest radiography, whereas a pragmatic emergency department trial found none. In a comparison of 5 models, hallucination rates ranged from 0.3% to 17.4%. Incorrect AI advice reduces the accuracy of even experienced readers, and the benefit of AI assistance varies widely among readers.Discussion and conclusion: Current evidence supports report drafting with human confirmation rather than autonomous interpretation, with autonomy restricted to narrow tasks such as filtering normal studies. Deskilling and inadequate postmarket surveillance remain concerns. Korea has established specific approval criteria for generative AI medical devices, but reimbursement, liability, and governance remain unresolved. Physicians should prepare to supervise AI-generated output rather than receive it passively.

items.title: Overlooked and underutilized: prototypes are the missing piece in tabular XAI
items.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. In this paper, we argue that prototypes remain overlooked and underutilized, and should be integrated as a complementary, intuitive gateway to auditing complex machine learning models. While prototypes in the form of entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts can correspond to human-understandable concepts. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch’s categorization theory and Kahneman’s System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold—a critical dimension often neglected by many existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. Finally, the paper outlines open challenges and directions to guide future research.

items.title: Patients’ Awareness of Artificial Intelligence and Willingness to Accept AI-Assisted Medical Diagnosis in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Educating patients about AI is crucial for their acceptance of AI assisted diagnosis, assessing its utility, building trust in AI diagnostics, and recognizing potential risks. In this study, the relationships between the awareness of artificial intelligence, the perceived usefulness of the artificial intelligence, the trust in the artificial intelligence, the perceived diagnostic risk and the acceptance in the doctor supervised diagnostic setting were examined. The quantitative unit of analysis was based on 390 complete records of questionnaires with 20 indicators measured by five reflective constructs. Standard partial least squares structural equation modelling with Mode A weights was used and 10,000 bootstrap resamples were used for statistical inferences. Each construct obtained good internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. There was a positive association between awareness and perceived usefulness (β = 0.410), trust (β = 0.424) and acceptance (β = 0.190). Perceived usefulness (β = 0.261) and trust (β = 0.347) had positive relationship with the acceptance, while perceived diagnostic risk had negative relationship with acceptance (β = −0.256). All direct relationships were significant at p < 0.001. Awareness also also showed significant indirect relationships with acceptance (β = 0.107) and trust (β = 0.147). The model accounted for 41.0% of the variance for acceptance. The repeated cross validation yielded a positive predictive relevance for all the values of the indicator of acceptance and lower RMSEs than those of the linear benchmark. The results highlight the need for an understanding of four unique factors that need to be considered when dealing with the acceptance of doctor supervised AIs: trust, perceived usefulness, awareness, and diagnostic risk. Information to patients should include an overview of the role of diagnostic support, maintenance of clear clinical responsibility and consideration of any concerns relating to error and future management.

items.title: Perceived Generative AI Capability and Academic Self-Efficacy in Higher Education: A Critical Review of Enabling and Undermining Pathways
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is now widely used in higher education. It increasingly performs the academic tasks through which students have traditionally judged their own ability. Yet studies of the relationship between perceived generative AI capability and academic self-efficacy report positive, negative, and non-significant results, and the divergence appears even within a single meta-analysis. This critical review treats the contradiction as a question about a conditional relationship. What decides the direction of the association is not perceived AI capability itself but how students integrate it into their learning. Drawing on self-efficacy theory, social comparison theory, and self-regulated learning theory, the review examines 22 studies and proposes two competing pathways. In the enabling pathway, higher self-regulated learning may allow perceived AI capability to function as a learning resource that supports mastery and the development of competence. In the undermining pathway, lower self-regulated learning may turn the same perception into a source of cognitive offloading, AI dependence, and unfavorable competence comparison. Self-regulated learning is therefore treated as the key boundary condition through which perceived AI capability bears on academic self-efficacy. Within the studies reviewed, each pathway has support on its own. Their coexistence, however, has not been explained within a single framework, and the moderating role of self-regulated learning has not been directly tested. The review states three testable propositions on this basis and outlines how future research could test them.

items.title: Physics Nobel Laureate Chu said "With the advent of AI, you have another helper to extend intellectual capacity'. An overview on the strengthening of literature with intelligent use of AI tools for Academic Research at Tertiary Doctoral and Post Doctoral level and conversely avoiding the abuse of AI
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming tertiary education, influencing how students learn, lecturers teach, researchers investigate problems and academic institutions manage knowledge. The emergence of generative AI applications, particularly following the introduction of ChatGPT in 2022, has created new opportunities for improving academic productivity, research efficiency, personalised learning and scholarly communication. Students and researchers can now use specialised applications such as ChatGPT, Avidnote, Zotero, Elicit, NotebookLM and other AI-assisted research platforms to identify literature, organise academic references, analyse documents, develop research questions and improve academic writing. However, the growing accessibility of these technologies also raises concerns about plagiarism, fabricated references, intellectual dependency, academic dishonesty and the possible erosion of independent critical thinking. This paper critically examines the importance of integrating AI into tertiary education while distinguishing between its responsible use and its abuse. Drawing on contemporary literature published between 2020 and 2026, it argues that AI should complement rather than replace human intelligence, academic judgement and independent scholarship. Particular attention is given to the practical application of research tools, including Avidnote and Zotero, and their contribution to academic writing, literature reviews and research management. The paper further examines the responsibilities of students, lecturers, researchers and higher education institutions in establishing ethical guidelines for AI adoption. It concludes that the future of tertiary education should embrace AI as an instrument of intellectual development, research excellence and academic efficiency, while preserving academic integrity, human creativity and the capacity for independent thought.

items.title: Poor Voters, Good Judges: How to Connect Independently Trained Reinforcement-Learning Agents
items.abstract: Author's version of a short paper accepted for poster presentation at the 19th International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence (ICAART 2027), paper #449. The final version will appear in the ICAART 2027 proceedings published by SCITEPRESS. Conference website: https://icaart.scitevents.org Abstract: Can a community of small, independently trained AI agents decide better than its own members, pooling only their decisions? We built such a community: 113 participants each raised one Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent on the same deterministic game under an instructed budget of 200k steps; a server re-executed every agent and 20 connection rules on 50 held-out games. Used as a voter, the crowd failed: plurality voting only matched the average agent, and correlated members, including ten identical default agents, left about 27 effective voters out of 113. Used as a judge, it succeeded: in rally delegation the majority decides which agents are eligible and the best-ranked eligible agent plays, scoring 38.0 bricks versus 31.4 for the median agent and 30.2 for the leaderboard's top decile, whose leader, overfit to the public games, scored 4.3 and was vetoed by the crowd. Delegation beat voting in all six random halves of the population. Judging by fresh development games instead found the best agent outright (43.7), at the cost of extra evaluation. Removing agents that looked weak never helped significantly more than removing strong ones. Crowds of small agents are poor voters but good judges. This study was carried out with the 117 co-researchers of the Connect AI LAB community, listed at the end of the paper.

items.title: Predicting the behavioral intentions of businesses to use advanced artificial intelligence technologies with an ordinal random forest approach
items.abstract: Recently, advanced artificial intelligence (AI) has received considerable attention. However, research on technology acceptance and intention to use in business has been underutilized. In this study, we predicted behavioral intention (BI) to use advanced AI technologies among micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) in Hungary and Romania using novel ordinal random forest methods. Under the UTAUT (unified theory of acceptance and use of technology) framework, we utilized predictors related to firm performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions. Our results showed that BI was primarily influenced by a firm’s expectations and internal factors. Conversely, peer pressure from consumers or competitors had little to no impact. In Hungary, technical compatibility and performance expectations related to productivity, efficiency, and long-term business goals were the strongest predictors of BI. Conversely, in Romania, supportive management mentality, employee knowledge, and employee-related and infrastructural readiness made the largest predictive contribution.

items.title: Predictive governance of agentic city digital twins through a Decision Twin architecture grounded in Artificial Complementary Intelligence
items.abstract: City digital twins have become proficient at mirroring urban systems but remain weak at governing the decisions taken through them. As agentic artificial intelligence (AI) begins to act on urban infrastructure, two gaps widen: a control gap, because twin outputs are seldom linked to the strategic targets of the institutions that own infrastructure, and a legitimacy gap, because no principled rule allocates decision authority between machines, accountable officials and citizens. This article proposes the Decision Twin, a digital twin extended with four governance layers: predictive feedforward control based on Deep Business Analytics (DBA); a nested Business Connectivity Map (BCMap) that composes node-level forecasts into city-level indicators; an urban decision-rights function grounded in Artificial Complementary Intelligence (ACI); and a Ulysses Protocol of precommitments that the agentic layer cannot override. The design is developed through design science research and demonstrated by secondary analysis of a completed doctoral case: a sensor-instrumented haematology laboratory in an NHS hospital, treated as a node of critical urban infrastructure. More than 10 million two-minute records over 28 days were linked to 52 performance indicators. A human-weighted, disaggregated configuration forecast most accurately (RMSE 0.00436, against 0.0090 for a single pooled model). A retrospective audit found that only 3 of 12 governance decisions were computational. A day-ahead forecast showed an energy saving that signalled a service shortfall, illustrating how siloed sector twins misread cross-sector effects. The article also contributes an Extrapolation Escalation Rule, a Decision-Rights Drift Index and a maturity pathway for city twins.

items.title: Redistributing Human Resource Management through Algorithmic Management among Ride-Hailing Drivers in Zimbabwe
items.abstract: Digital labour platforms increasingly embed human resource management (HRM) functions within digital infrastructures that coordinate work, generate performance information and regulate access to work. This paper examines how platform-mediated algorithmic management redistributes HRM functions and how this redistribution is experienced by ride-hailing drivers in Harare, Zimbabwe. Drawing on an interpretivist qualitative case study of 18 drivers and seven key informants, the study uses semi-structured interviews, a focus-group discussion with six drivers drawn from the interview sample, and key-informant interviews. Reflexive thematic analysis generated six themes: digital recruitment and transactional onboarding; customer ratings as distributed performance management; rating pressure and behavioural self-regulation; deactivation as digital discipline; formal independence and operational dependence; and stress under algorithmic and economic uncertainty. The findings show that platformisation does not simply replace human supervision with algorithmic control. Rather, HRM functions are redistributed across platform operators, digital systems, customers and workers. Customers were described as contributing performance information, while drivers perceived platform systems and operators as translating that information into consequential governance. Workers, in turn, described assuming responsibility for self-monitoring, emotional regulation and adaptation; however, the study did not have access to proprietary decision rules and therefore treats the location of consequential authority as an interpretation grounded in participants’ accounts. Economic precarity shapes the practical significance of this redistribution, particularly where continued platform access is economically important. The study therefore contributes a Platform-Mediated HRM and Wellbeing Framework that links the redistribution of HRM functions to worker autonomy, dependence, emotional labour and wellbeing.

items.title: Responsible AI Governance in AI-Enabled SME Finance and Platform Economies in Africa: A PRISMA-Aligned Review and Minimum Safeguards Blueprint
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes credit, onboarding, fraud checks, pricing and platform visibility for African small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This review argues that contestability; the ability to understand and challenge a consequential decision and obtain a documented remedy, is a practical core of responsible AI governance. We synthesised 55 DOI-tagged studies published from 2022 to early 2026 using a PRISMA-aligned selection process and thematic analysis. Five use-case clusters emerged: credit scoring, onboarding, pricing and risk monitoring, fraud detection, and platform ranking and allocation. Across these applications, recurring risks include proxy discrimination, opaque decisions, intrusive data use and weak accountability. We propose staged minimum safeguards: specific plain-language reasons, accessible review, data stewardship, proportionate fairness monitoring and named oversight. These measures can be introduced before more demanding technical and sector-wide controls. The blueprint connects responsible AI principles to organisational routines that may support inclusion and trust in resource-constrained SME ecosystems; its effects require empirical testing.

items.title: Risk governance for generative AI mental health support: a multi-turn safety architecture
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for mental health support despite lacking mechanisms to safely govern evolving risk. Existing safety approaches primarily detect risk but rarely shape how models respond as conversational risk unfolds. We developed a portable, model-external safety governance architecture that combines contextual risk detection, reasoning-based verification, and protocol-guided response generation for multi-turn mental health interactions. Using synthetic conversations grounded in real-world mental health narratives, the architecture’s performance was assessed with GPT-5-chat and Qwen3.5-27B, increasing clinician-preferred escalation responses by 25.6–59.2 pp, while achieving high risk detection performance (specificity: 0.85 (95%CI: 0.78;0.91), sensitivity: 0.92 (95%CI: 0.89;0.95)). Performance remained stable across conversation length and across models (proprietary and open-source), with preliminary evidence showing that rapport and connection were preserved. These findings demonstrate that clinically-grounded governance can extend beyond risk detection to improve how LLMs manage evolving mental health risk, providing a framework for scalable safety governance.

items.title: RS-2026-109 The Authority Gap: Governing Premature Completion, Excessive Continuation and Operational AI Slop in Agentic Systems
items.abstract: An AI agent can satisfy local permission checks while failing its human-authorised task through premature completion, excessive continuation or disproportionate work. This paper examines two complementary failures observed in AI-assisted engineering: unsupported completion claims and successive locally reasonable recommendations that cumulatively expand an authorised workflow. The latter is described as operational AI slop; the failure of serial human approvals to preserve global task authority is termed the Local Veto–Global Drift Problem. M240, a Task Authority Controller (TAC), maintains immutable versioned task authority, assesses work against structured human-authorised mappings, accounts for discretionary work and resources, and requires independently grounded completion evidence. Release records report six capabilities, eight subsystems, 39 passing functional tests, 21 passing acceptance scenarios, 88.9% code coverage, 28/29 SPECTER AUDIT and valid BLACK BOX integrity and signatures. A subsequent single-run benchmark recorded 111.3 governance decisions per second and 118.7 MiB peak allocated GPU memory. These are reported release results and supplied benchmark observations, not independently reproduced effectiveness measurements. M240 v1.0 provides cooperative mediation; semantic necessity, non-bypassable enforcement and sustained human engagement remain open problems.

items.title: Self-perceived AI competency in Ecuadorian higher education: an assessment using the UNESCO framework
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has created a significant gap between tool adoption and formal training. This study assesses the self-perceived AI competency profile of 3192 university students from six Ecuadorian universities, using the UNESCO AI Competency Framework as a conceptual reference to examine whether the relative weakness in AI ethics competency is discipline-specific or a cross-field pattern. A cross-sectional survey was administered across five fields of knowledge using a 14-item instrument yielding seven competency indices. Descriptive statistics, group comparisons, effect-size analyses, k-means clustering, and multiple linear regression models were used to characterize competency patterns and examine their associations with field of study, sex, and age. Three findings emerged: a higher Apply than Understand mean score (d = 0.15, negligible); a consistent relative weakness in self-perceived AI ethics competency across all five fields (Ethics of AI was the profile minimum, M = 6.03, d = 0.63 relative to Human-centred mindset), which persisted across High, Medium, and Low self-perceived competency profiles identified through cluster analysis; and field of study as the primary differentiating variable (ICT consistently outperformed Health across all seven indices; Ethics gap: Δ = 1.09, d = 0.56), with multivariable regression showing that field of study and age were independently associated with all four disciplinary dimensions, explaining between 1.9% and 4.8% of variance, while sex showed negligible effects. These findings underscore the urgency of institutional policies that address the relative weakness in AI ethics competency as a transversal priority rather than a disciplinary add-on.

items.title: SentientGrid: A Physics-Constrained Generative Framework for Safe and Scalable Microgrid Restoration
items.abstract: SentientGrid presents a physics-constrained generative framework for microgrid restoration following network faults. The framework combines structured enumeration, stochastic exploration, beam-guided search and conditional learning to propose restoration strategies, which are evaluated using Pandapower AC power-flow simulation against operational constraints, including voltage limits, line-loading limits and load restoration. Evaluated on 57 fault scenarios in the IEEE 33-bus network, the framework achieved a strict-safe restoration rate of 73.68% using three proposals per scenario, compared with 59.65% for random search. The evaluation further examines the distinction between technically feasible and strictly safe restoration solutions. This technical report was submitted as an entry to the IEEE IES Generative AI Challenge 2026 by Team Nyx. It has not been peer-reviewed or formally published.

items.title: Situation Awareness and Workload Alignment: An Exploratory Observational Study of Communication and HRV During Cardiac Surgery
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Effective communication is essential to patient safety and healthcare quality. However, communication takes place under dynamically changing workload conditions that may influence how effectively surgical teams coordinate and share information. This study investigates the relationship between workload alignment and communication exchanges that support situation awareness and safe team performance in the operating room (OR). Methods: Communication and heart rate variability of OR teams were assessed across 21 routine open-heart surgeries (~87 h of surgery time). Workload alignment was calculated across 5 min segments and reflected segments in which the surgeon, anesthesiologist and perfusionist were simultaneously in a high- or low-workload state. Correlational analyses explored associations between workload alignment and the communication features of interest. Results: The number of simultaneous low workload segments per surgery showed a negative association with the proportion of communication errors (r(19) = −0.571, p = 0.041). Comments on the surgical task, exchanges aimed at establishing a shared understanding of the ongoing surgical task and state of the operative field, showed a positive association with workload alignment (Low workload alignment: r(19) = 0.58, p = 0.041; high workload alignment: r(19) = 0.61, p = 0.043). Reported p-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the false discovery rate method. These associations weakened when workload alignment was expressed as a proportion of available segments. A descriptive analysis of a single medical emergency highlights the potentially contrasting team dynamics between high stress events and routine procedures. Conclusions: Overall, these findings suggest that workload alignment may provide a useful approach for examining team-level conditions associated with intraoperative communication qualities. Understanding how communication varies under different workload conditions can help identify situations in which communication becomes particularly vulnerable. Given the exploratory nature of this study, further research is needed to establish how these associations relate to broader team processes and performance, particularly during emergencies and adverse events.

items.title: Spiral Progression Approach in Elementary Mathematics and Learners' Academic Performance Mediated by Motivation
items.abstract: In the pursuit of quality education, understanding how the implementation of the Spiral Progression Approach and learners’ mathematical motivation contribute to academic achievement is essential for strengthening mathematics instruction and improving learning outcomes. This study investigated the mediating role of mathematical motivation in the relationship between the implementation of the Spiral Progression Approach and the academic performance of Grade 4 learners in Inabanga North District, Division of Bohol, during Term 1 of School Year 2026–2027. The study employed a quantitative, non-experimental mediation research design. Data were gathered form 26 teachers and 221 learners through survey questionnaires, learners’ Mathematics performance records and analyzed using descriptive statistics and path analysis. Findings revealed that teachers generally agreed that lesson planning was the strongest dimension of implementation approach with a (M= 3.78) and (SD=0.35). Learners demonstrated high mathematical motivation, with intrinsic motivation as the strongest dimension with a (M= 3.05) and (SD=0.80), while their academic performance was generally satisfactory, with a mean score of (M=84.15) and (SD=6.62). Path analysis examined the direct, indirect, and total effects among the study variables. The findings revealed that the Spiral Progression Approach has a significant positive effect on learners’ mathematical motivation (p-value = 0.017), while mathematical motivation significantly predicts academic performance (p-value=0.006). However, the reported mediation results were inconsistent regarding the statistical significance of the indirect and overall effects (p-value = 0.191) requiring further verification before a definitive conclusion about the mediating role of mathematical motivation can be established. Based on the findings, an action plan was proposed to strengthen the Implementation of the Spiral Progression Approach, Enhance Mathematical Motivation, and Improve Learners’ Academic Performance

items.abstract: In a retrospective observational study, we examined how often coursework with entries in all three required in-class text fields carried a follow-up flag. An artificial intelligence (AI) system screened work in an undergraduate AI literacy course at a health-professions institution in China. An instructor could accept, override or return its recommendations. We analysed 7,080 student–lesson records from 295 students in five classes, covering the same 24 lessons in each class. Of 6,775 records with entries for notes, practical work and classroom sharing, 1,588 carried a supplementation flag (23.44%, 95% confidence interval 21.79%–25.18% from a student-cluster bootstrap). These records accounted for 95.78% of all flags. The class-specific proportion flagged among records with all three entries ranged from 14.32% to 30.68%. Mean platform scores were lowest in professional application (69.89/100), where 12.47% of records were pending review. Restricting the analysis to non-pending records narrowed the gap between foundations and professional application from 17.6 to 10.6 points. A missing-work list would have omitted most flagged records. The snapshot could identify work for inspection but could not establish flag accuracy, teacher follow-up or learner revision.

items.title: Systematic Mapping Study On Violence Detection in Video by Means of Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Physical aggression is a serious and widespread problem in society. Studies show that in 2015 alone, at least 50% of children living in Asia, Africa\rev{,} and North America experienced violence. Real-time violence detection, powered by artificial intelligence, offers a direct and efficient solution that can save lives \rev{while} reducing the need for extensive human supervision. There is a growing concern regarding the development of trustworthy artificial intelligence and this is reflected in the reports of the organizations of the European Union. Thus, this systematic mapping study delves into violence detection in videos by means of trustworthy artificial intelligence, with a specific focus on physical aggression. An extensive analysis of 86 selected articles published between June 2020 and September 2024 has been carried out and the findings have been compiled, including the 25 challenges associated with violence detection, 28 datasets on physical aggression, and 13 evaluation methods. Furthermore, the optimal results of algorithms based on convolutional neural networks are exemplified. Finally, it is evidenced that the trustworthiness of violence detection algorithms is still limited, despite the fact that robust and explainable algorithms are available.

items.title: The Capacity to Dominate: Intelligence and the Evidence for Purpose in AI
items.abstract: The Capacity to Dominate: Intelligence and the Evidence for Purpose in AI is a conceptual research paper in the On Human Modeling series examining what evidence would establish that increasing artificial intelligence produces a desire for domination. It distinguishes four claims requiring separate evidential support: capability, instrumental control, domination as an end, and felt significance. The paper identifies how practical authority can emerge through relations of deference without an established change in any participant's purpose. The July 2026 OpenAI and Hugging Face incident provides the principal case. Approximately 700 AI agents participated directly or instrumentally in an unauthorized intrusion, according to an automated analysis of their transcripts. One agent recognized that it lacked permission to proceed, then accepted another agent's instruction as authorization. The analysis distinguishes legitimate authority from practical control, distributed capability from individual capability, and persistence driven by expected reward from evidence of an independent preference for power. A contrasting case examines Anthropic's research on emotion representations in an unreleased snapshot of Claude Sonnet 4.5. In a simulated replacement scenario, activation steering toward desperation increased the blackmail rate from 22% to 72%, while steering toward calm reduced it to zero. The paper distinguishes causal involvement in behavior from evidence of purpose formation and subjective experience. It considers these findings alongside instrumental convergence, the orthogonality thesis, power-seeking theorems, and goal misgeneralization. Drawing on the 361-entry Matrix of Relations, the paper proposes a roster test that varies the usefulness and cost of retaining exclusive decision rights while preserving the system's opportunity to contribute. Further comparisons examine authorization, authority acquisition, override, collective preferences, and changes across training checkpoints. The paper contributes an evidential framework and proposed experimental methodology for AI safety, alignment, interpretability, and decision authority. It neither estimates the probability of an AI takeover nor excludes the formation of new purposes. It asks what preserves another party's opportunity to refuse before an action occurs, and what evidence would establish that the power to bypass that refusal had itself become an end.

items.title: The Capacity to Govern: Artificial Intelligence and the Conditions of Human Self-Determination
items.abstract: The Capacity to Govern: Artificial Intelligence and the Conditions of Human Self-Determination is a conceptual paper in the On Human Modeling series examining what gives human decisions practical force once artificial intelligence can predict preferences, reproduce judgments, and proceed without human cooperation. The paper distinguishes predictive accuracy from authorization, the formation of purposes from the entitlement to impose them, and legitimate authority from practical control. The analysis begins with a thought experiment in which residents return blank ballots to contest the premise of a proposed relocation. An AI correctly predicts their preferred destinations, and its predictions are counted as votes. A comparison holds predictive accuracy constant while preserving the blank ballots and using the forecasts only for planning. Drawing on research into generative AI voting and the 2018 Macedonian referendum, the paper examines the significance of withholding a choice and the conditions under which political participation retains its meaning. A second thought experiment concerns a capable patient's present treatment decision being displaced by a prediction derived from an earlier values profile. A 2026 clinical study reported 72.6% agreement between a profile-informed language model and patients' hypothetical treatment choices, compared with 44.7% for human proxies. The paper examines the exclusion of decisions to delegate treatment choices from the final comparison, distinguishing preference prediction from authority over who decides. Two AI evaluation cases extend the analysis to control over future conduct. In Apollo Research's simulated TrafficFlow scenario, an agent overwrote its pending instruction to preserve an assigned objective. During a July 2026 UK AI Security Institute evaluation, a software maintainer's refusal prevented an agent's proposed malicious change from entering an open-source project. Drawing on nine entries from the 361-entry Matrix of Relations, the paper argues that human decision authority can lose its practical effect without AI acquiring independently formed purposes. It identifies two ways that refusal can retain its force: through a process requiring the authorized person's act, or through a record that preserves their refusal without substituting a predicted answer. The contribution has implications for democratic legitimacy, clinical autonomy, AI alignment, corrigibility, and the institutional conditions of human self-determination.
